report:
The fault-injection phase failed to maintain the frontendDeploymentAvailableReplicas steady state. The measured availability was 91.11%, below the required 99% threshold, meaning that for approximately 8.9% of the 360-second fault-injection period (about 32 one-second observations) the front-end Deployment had zero available replicas. This directly violates the steady-state assertion and disproves the hypothesis that the system remains stable under the injected faults.

Root causes are directly tied to the front-end Deployment configuration and the fault sequence. The front-end Deployment (sock-shop-2/manifests/09-front-end-dep.yaml) runs exactly 1 replica (spec.replicas: 1). This makes the front-end pod a single point of failure: whenever that pod is killed, unhealthy, or not ready, there are no other pods to serve traffic, and availableReplicas drops to 0. The fault scenario deliberately targeted this single pod with three consecutive fault blocks: (1) StressChaos injecting 100% CPU load and 256MB memory stress; (2) NetworkChaos injecting 50% packet loss “to” the front-end pod; (3) PodChaos pod-kill on the front-end pod. The front-end container has resource limits of cpu: 1000m and memory: 512Mi, and it runs a web server on port 8079. Under CPU/memory stress, the existing readiness and liveness probes (httpGet on /, port 8079) can time out or fail, causing Kubernetes to mark the pod as unready or restart it. Under 50% packet loss, probes from the kubelet can also fail intermittently, leading to repeated unavailability and restarts. Most decisively, the pod-kill fault removes the only front-end replica. After a kill, Kubernetes must schedule and start a new pod, and the readiness probe has initialDelaySeconds: 30, so the replacement pod is not considered available for at least 30 seconds (plus container startup/image-pull time). Thus a single pod-kill alone can produce a 30-60 second outage, which in a 360-second observation window corresponds to ~8-16% unavailability—enough to fail the 99% requirement. The observed ~32 zero-value seconds are consistent with a combination of stress-induced probe failures, network-loss-induced restarts, and the pod-kill recovery delay.

Additionally, the steady-state threshold also requires no consecutive zero observations longer than 1 second; a pod-kill recovery inherently takes many seconds, so this condition was certainly violated as well, even though the script reported the ratio assertion first.

To improve resiliency and prevent this failure, the following changes are recommended:
- Increase the replica count for the front-end Deployment to at least 2 (ideally 3) so that the service remains available during a pod kill or node failure. The Service selector only matches the front-end pod label, and with multiple replicas the Service will send traffic to the healthy ones.
- Add a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) for the front-end Deployment to guarantee a minimum number of available replicas during voluntary disruptions.
- Consider configuring anti-affinity or pod distribution constraints so that replicas are spread across different nodes, protecting against node-level failures.
- For stress/load resilience, configure a HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) based on CPU/memory usage so the deployment can scale out before becoming saturated.
- Review and tune the readiness and liveness probe settings (e.g., timeoutSeconds, periodSeconds, failureThreshold) so transient CPU spikes or packet loss do not cause the sole replica to be marked unready unnecessarily; however, with multiple replicas, even if one pod is temporarily unready the steady-state availability is maintained.
- The front-end container should not be a single point of failure; the above scaling and distribution changes directly address the observed failure and are sufficient to pass the steady-state threshold under the given fault scenario.
